query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small, controlled amount of interstitial carbon into equimolar CoCrFeNiTi promotes optimal short‐range order and increases lattice distortions, which in turn enhances the resistance to dislocation motion, leading to improved hardness and compressive strength while retaining good plasticity.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state with favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled concentration (e.g., tentatively 0.5–1.0 at.% C) of interstitial carbon during alloy synthesis without triggering the formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted on samples processed under identical conditions at room temperature and up to 600 °C under standard compressive loading rates, ensuring that the alloy remains in its solid-solution state.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortions and induced short-range order (SRO) within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial carbon increases local lattice distortions and optimizes SRO, which raises the energy barrier against leading dislocation motion and promotes back stresses through antiphase boundary formation, thereby boosting solid-solution strengthening. This mechanism is expected to improve hardness and compressive strength by impeding dislocation glide without significantly reducing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped CoCrFeNiTi alloy will exhibit measurably higher hardness and compressive strength compared to the baseline alloy, while maintaining or only modestly reducing its ductility. The magnitude of property improvement is uncertain and requires calibration, but a statistically significant enhancement is anticipated under controlled testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Undoped CoCrFeNiTi prepared as an equimolar solid solution, exhibiting good plasticity and machinability but lower hardness and strength.
generation.boundary: Applicable to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloys processed to retain a simple solid-solution FCC structure, with tests performed from room temperature up to 600 °C under standard mechanical loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal carbon concentration to achieve the desired balance of increased strength and retained ductility is not precisely known, and excessive carbon could lead to carbide precipitation or embrittlement. The quantitative improvement in mechanical properties also requires experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNiTi alloy samples using identical processing routes (e.g., mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering): one set as a baseline with no carbon addition, and another with a controlled interstitial carbon addition (0.5–1.0 at.%). Characterize both sets to confirm the retention of a single-phase FCC solid solution. Conduct systematic mechanical tests (hardness measurements, compressive tests) at room temperature and 600 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in hardness and compressive strength (or if they exhibit a detrimental drop in ductility) compared to the undoped baseline, the hypothesis that controlled interstitial carbon enhances strengthening via SRO and lattice distortions will be falsified.

Tuning the stability of the face-centered cubic (f.c.c.) matrix phase in the dual-phase structure to a critical point triggers the twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) effect while maintaining the TRIP effect, thereby further improving the alloy’s strain-hardening ability,. Second, HEAs benefit profoundly from interstitial solid solution strengthening instead of only the established massive solid solution strengthening provided by its multiple principle elements,. This is due to the circumstance that carbon, nitrogen and other interstitials lead to much higher lattice distortions than substitutional elements which strongly affects their interaction with dislocations,. The improved mechanical properties (Fig. 3) and the associated multiple deformation mechanisms (Fig. 4) confirm the success of the new design approach, and its potential economic viability since interstitial alloying elements are much cheaper compared to substitutional alloying elements. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEAs unify all known metallurgical strengthening effects in one single bulk material: i) massive substitutional solid solution strengthening due to multiple principle elements (i.e., Fe, Mn, Co and Cr); ii) interstitial solid solution strengthening by carbon; iii) micro-composite effect from dual-phase structure; iv) nano-particle strengthening from nano-carbides (Figs 2b and 4c); v) nano-twinning induced plasticity effect (TWIP) (Fig. 4b); vi) displacive transformation induced plasticity effect (TRIP) (Fig. 4a); vii) formation of stacking faults (Fig. 4b); viii) grain size reduction (increased grain boundary density); and dislocation hardening (Fig. 4b).

At a given temperature and strain rate, the strength of MPEAs is dictated by dislocation motion–related solid solution strengthening and grain size–dependent Hall-Petch effect. In the presence of SRO and, consequently, high SFE (, ), it is reasonable to speculate that the motion of leading partial will experience a large resistance and high energy barrier. In addition, the following passage of trailing partial, when it happens, can erase the SF and restore the fcc structure but inevitably create a diffuse antiphase boundary owing to the destruction of SRO on the slip plane. The interplay between SF creation, antiphase boundary generation, and the associated energy penalty, stemming from the existence of SRO, exerts back stress on moving dislocation and retards its motion, which is the root cause of enhanced solid solution strengthening. The Hall-Petch strengthening is influenced by SRO in a way that the critical grain size (strongest size) corresponding to the maximum strength decreases to a smaller value, accompanied by deferred strength softening (Fig. 1E). reading.lever: Introduce controlled interstitial carbon to promote optimal SRO and lattice distortions in CoCrFeNiTi.
reading.why: This lever, demonstrated in TRIP-DP-HEAs, can bolster hardness and strength without forming brittle intermetallics, directly addressing the mechanical limitations of the solid solution state.
